suppressed_questions.question: Liner condition and flue count
suppressed_questions.why_suppressed: The chimney is out of service and enclosed. Liner status is irrelevant to a stabilization scope, and caps are priced per flue on a chimney that vents nothing.
suppressed_questions.note: The standard chimney checklist asks this. Asking it here would cost Dan credibility with a client he has just spent an hour with.

suppressed_questions.question: Crown rebuild vs repair
suppressed_questions.why_suppressed: Deferred, not suppressed. A crown on a dead chimney is a water-shedding element, still worth doing — but it is subordinate to the crack scope and cannot be sized until the top condition is described.

refusals.position: NOT PRICED — and will not be until a rental yard quotes it.
refusals.reason: Dan said plainly that he has not called anyone. Any figure the tool produced here would be a fabrication wearing the costume of an estimate, and it sits on the largest uncertainty in the job. The tool instead produces a call sheet specifying exactly what to ask for.
refusals.what_it_produces_instead: Equipment call sheet with the machine class, the site constraints to quote against, and the questions that determine whether the machine can be sited at all.

refusals.reason: Was: not derivable from 'big cracks around the top'. Dan supplied the quantity. Note it describes MORTAR JOINT cracking, which the repoint line covers — no separate stone crack repair line is carried.
'Twenty plus feet' spans a real cost range once access equipment is sized to it. Lift working height is specified in fixed increments and the wrong increment is the wrong machine.

Was: 'historical' describes the chimney, which is not the same as a designated property. Dan confirmed the property is not on a register. The 15–25% factor does not apply, and the removal alternative can be raised freely.

refusals.position: NOT REFUSED — and it should have been.
refusals.reason: The tool assumed 44 sq ft (an 11 ft perimeter over the top 4 ft) to price the largest masonry line. Nobody measured it and nothing implied it. Recorded here as a failure of the refusal rule, not a success of it: the rule caught what Dan flagged as unknown and missed what he simply did not mention. The line is marked contingent and the assumption is stated, but that is mitigation, not a defence.
refusals.what_it_produces_instead: Flagged high-severity in open items, and first on the site-visit measure list.

surfaced_for_dan.finding: The chimney is non-functional and enclosed. Nobody uses it. The client's stated goal is that it stop deteriorating.
surfaced_for_dan.implication: Repairing masonry at 20+ ft solves that goal for as long as the repair holds, on a structure exposed to 100+ freeze-thaw cycles a year with no heat ever passing through it. Taking the chimney down to the roofline and capping the opening solves it permanently, needs no lift at full height, and is very likely cheaper.
surfaced_for_dan.instruction: This is not the tool overriding Dan. It is a scope alternative the memo implies and the client may not have considered. Dan decides whether to raise it; if the property is designated or the client values the silhouette, it is off the table immediately.
surfaced_for_dan.caveat: Historic district status has since been confirmed as NOT designated, so removal is not blocked by review. That clears the regulatory objection but not the aesthetic one — it is the client's house and the client's skyline. Raise it as an option, once, and drop it if the answer is no.

surfaced_for_dan.finding: Working alone at 20+ ft, hoisting ~30 lb stone from a platform, on a machine sited on uneven unpaved ground.
surfaced_for_dan.implication: This is the safety question Dan raised twice in ninety seconds. It bears on machine selection — a platform with a material rack and adequate capacity, not the cheapest lift that reaches — and on whether a tender for the lift days is worth pricing in even though he says he has no reliable helper.
surfaced_for_dan.instruction: Priced options should reflect this. The cheapest access is not the correct access.

surfaced_for_dan.finding: Heavily wooded site. Nothing in the memo addresses what is directly above the chimney.
surfaced_for_dan.implication: RESOLVED — Dan confirmed nothing overhead. Boom articulation unobstructed, no limb removal, no client permission needed.
surfaced_for_dan.instruction: Closed. Retained here to show the question was asked and answered rather than dropped.

surfaced_for_dan.finding: Narrow, uneven, unpaved, landscaped flagstone approach.
surfaced_for_dan.implication: A conventional self-propelled boom is likely both too wide and too heavy — it will crack the flagstone. The machine class that exists for exactly this problem is a tracked or 'spider' lift: narrow enough for pedestrian paths, low ground pressure, outriggers that level on uneven ground.
surfaced_for_dan.instruction: Named on the call sheet so Dan asks the rental yard the right question rather than an open one.

surfaced_for_dan.finding: The access route is finished landscaping, not a driveway.
surfaced_for_dan.implication: Damage to the client's flagstone path during access is a foreseeable cost. Left unaddressed it becomes an argument at the end of the job.
surfaced_for_dan.instruction: Either a protection allowance in the scope or an explicit exclusion in the proposal. Not silence.

open_questions.q: Roughly how many linear feet of cracking, total?
open_questions.why: Primary quantity. Stone crack repair prices per linear foot ($22–45/lin ft).
open_questions.answered: Under 10 lin ft — mortar joint cracking

open_questions.q: Is it cracks only, or are stones actually loose or displaced?
open_questions.why: Crack repair, unit reset ($120–350 each), and dutchman ($220–700 each) are three different jobs at three different prices.
open_questions.answered: Mortar joint cracks plus some stones possibly shifted; not conclusive

open_questions.q: How much of the chimney needs work — just the top few feet, or more of it?
open_questions.why: Determines whether this is spot crack repair or a repoint of the upper section ($18–30/sq ft fieldstone).

open_questions.q: What's the very top doing — is there a cap or crown, and is it intact?
open_questions.why: An open top on a dead chimney is a water funnel. Cheap to address while the lift is there; expensive to return for.

open_questions.q: How wide is that path, and how far from where a truck can park to the chimney?
open_questions.why: Determines machine class and whether it can be sited at all.

open_questions.q: Is the property actually in a designated historic district?
open_questions.why: 15–25% factor plus review timeline, and it governs whether the removal option can even be discussed.

open_questions.q: When does the client want this done?
open_questions.why: Nov–Mar adds 18–28% and masonry cannot be laid in freezing temperatures at all.
open_questions.answered: Before winter, not urgent; client taking multiple bids
